questions.prompt: A JWT consists of three base64url parts separated by dots:
questions.explain: **header.payload.signature** — each base64url encoded; the signature = HMAC of the first two parts with the server secret.

questions.source: MCQ Bank Q40 — the 401 vs 403 question
questions.prompt: A logged-in member (role=member) sends a VALID token with `DELETE /api/books/1`, which requires admin. The correct response is:
questions.explain: **Valid token (authenticated) but insufficient role → 403 Forbidden.** 401 = missing/invalid token (unauthenticated). Memorize this pair — it's the classic JWT exam question.

questions.prompt: Why can the server trust a JWT WITHOUT a database lookup?
options: The signature is an HMAC over header.payload with the server's secret — any tampering with the payload invalidates it
The token is encrypted so nobody can read it
The payload is stored in the session
questions.explain: JWTs are **signed, not encrypted** — anyone can READ the payload (base64url), but only the secret-holder can produce a valid signature. Change one byte of the payload and verification fails. That's stateless auth.

options: A Unix timestamp (issued time + TTL) after which decode/validation rejects the token
questions.explain: **exp = $now + ttl** (e.g. 3600s). Validation rejects expired tokens automatically — the client must log in again (or refresh). sub carries the user id; role is a custom claim baked at login.

questions.prompt: The client sends the JWT on every protected request via:
questions.explain: **`Authorization: Bearer <token>`** — which is also why the CORS preflight must allow the Authorization header. Middleware regex: `/^Bearer\s+(.+)$/i`.

questions.prompt: Why does `JWT::decode` require `new Key($secret, 'HS256')` instead of just the secret?
options: Pinning the algorithm prevents algorithm-swap attacks (e.g. an attacker setting alg:none or downgrading)
questions.explain: The Key object pins secret **AND algorithm** — the historic JWT vulnerability was servers honoring the header's `alg` field (`none`/downgrade attacks). Never trust the token to tell you how to verify it.

questions.prompt: A request arrives with NO token at all on a protected route. Which status code? (number)
questions.explain: **401 Unauthorized** (+ `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`) = unauthenticated. 403 = authenticated but lacking the role.

questions.prompt: Order-check: the correct LOGIN flow is —
options: POST /login → verify password_verify → build payload (sub, role, exp) → JWT::encode → return token → client stores it and sends Bearer header on each request
POST /login → store password in the token → client re-sends the password each time
Client builds the token itself → server trusts the role claim
questions.explain: Login: verify against the bcrypt hash → mint the signed token with sub/role/exp → client keeps it and presents `Authorization: Bearer` per request → middleware verifies signature + expiry, attaches the payload, handlers check the role. The client can never mint or alter tokens (no secret).
